A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SOS-BENCH and LLM-judge bias study. Their text, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison despite the revised title and added analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original judge-intervention experiments, post-training evaluations, and model, decoding and authority-bias ablations.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds comparisons across judges, evaluation-pipeline ablations and factor analysis.

M1.justification: The SOS-BENCH aggregation, five-criterion judging prompt and post-training procedures are retained. The new pipeline variants and factor analysis extend evaluation without changing the proposed benchmark or canonical judging procedure.

E1.justification: v3 adds a question-domain test using nontechnical Reddit questions, including AskHistorians, and a BenchBench agreement analysis covering additional leaderboards. The SOS-BENCH datasets in Table 8 and the training-data coverage remain unchanged.

E2.justification: v3 Figure 2 adds GPT-4-Turbo to the response-model comparison corresponding to v1 Table 2. The specialist and preference-optimization comparator sets remain unchanged. Code Llama 3, Numina Math CoT and Tulu Human are newly listed in Table 7 but were already evaluated in v1 Table 4.

E3.justification: v3 adds a four-judge evaluation and progressive Arena-Hard-Auto variants that alter response-order controls, self-generated reference answers, judging templates, reference models and questions. Appendix K adds an analysis using 12,000 judgments per criterion, recoded to a five-point scale. These substantially expand the evaluation design; the existing training settings and SOS-BENCH metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether criterion weighting persists across judges (Table 2), which pipeline choices affect scores and rankings (Appendix I.3), and how judgment criteria overlap (Appendix K). These substantially extend the retained model, decoding, chat-template and authority-bias ablations.

E5.justification: v3 Table 2 newly reports standard deviations across judges, and Appendix K adds Bartlett's sphericity test and factor-analysis estimates. Existing 95% confidence-interval reporting is retained. The PDFs do not establish an increase in repeated training runs or seeds.

E6.justification: v3 replaces the criterion scores in v1 Table 2 with different Figure 2 results and adds cross-judge correlations, including style Pearson correlation 0.999, pipeline-ablation scores and factor loadings. It also adds BenchBench aggregates, revises Zephyr and WizardLM classifications in Table 7, and removes the earlier survey percentages. Core SOS-BENCH results remain unchanged. Figure 2's judge and reference conditions are inconsistently documented, preventing same-setting performance comparisons.

T1.justification: The operational mapping between HHH principles and benchmark factors is retained. Neither version develops formal theorems or proofs, and v3's factor analysis adds empirical statistical analysis rather than new mathematical theory.

C1.justification: The abstract weakens v1's claim that SFT, rather than preference optimization, has the greatest alignment impact to the claim that SFT has a large impact. The introduction also more explicitly scopes judge-bias claims to alignment benchmarking. The central benchmark and stylistic-bias contributions remain.

C2.justification: Appendix K introduces a shared Quality interpretation for correctness, completeness and style, alongside Accuracy and Brevity components and largely separate safety judgments. Appendix I.3 interprets limited sensitivity to question domains as a concern for specialized applications. v3 also acknowledges imperfect reference labels and dependence between judgment criteria, substantially extending v1's interpretation of stylistic reward hacking.

D1.justification: v3 replaces the anonymous code pointer with a named GitHub repository and adds a reproducibility statement identifying sources and checkpoint-release intentions. Appendix K documents Likert recoding, MINRES estimation, Varimax rotation and the eigenvalue threshold; Appendix B adds the four-judge comparison's $600 API cost. Existing training hyperparameters remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds BenchBench, Wu and Aji's evaluation-bias work, and Sorensen et al.'s pluralistic-alignment work, plus references for already evaluated Code Llama 3 and Numina Math. These improve coverage of relevant research without substantially redefining the paper's novelty or positioning.

P1.justification: v3 changes the title to Style Outweighs Substance, clarifies preference-benchmark terminology, rewrites Section 3, shortens the recommendations and adds a reproducibility section. Most existing prose and the overall section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: The central criterion-score table becomes a scatterplot, accompanied by a new cross-judge correlation table. v3 also adds the pipeline-ablation heatmap and factor-analysis tables, substantially expanding the visual evidence. Figure 1's caption and Table 7 are revised; the existing scaling plots are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v1's criterion-weighting finding depended on one judge configuration. v3's four-judge comparison and pipeline ablations substantially strengthen its support and test previously conjectured confounds. The factor analysis qualifies criterion independence, and the softened SFT claim improves calibration. Figure 2 introduces reporting ambiguities and loses the earlier table's numerical precision, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in robustness evidence and interpretation.
